solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ornamental moulding: mine also rancho adapted

indicators.note: something adapted has been altered to suit, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: egg is old military slang for a mine or bomb
'and' and 'also' both add one thing to another
the six letters of rancho rearranged

explanation.surface: A description of a decorative feature on a ranch house, with a mine thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg-and-anchor is a classical architectural moulding of alternating egg and dart-like shapes, a variant of egg-and-dart.

clue.text: I fancy roadkill — it's swell devouring monster

indicators.note: something devouring takes food inside itself, so the first word swallows the second

parts.note: to swell is to grow larger
an orc is an ogre or monster of folklore and Tolkien

explanation.surface: Someone confesses a taste for animals killed on the road, while a monster swells as it gorges.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken by the bird itself: the gorcrow is the carrion crow, which feeds on dead animals such as roadkill.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorcrow is an old name for the carrion crow, a scavenger whose diet of dead flesh includes animals killed by traffic.

clue.text: Gorge on energy, creating muscle

parts.note: to glut is to gorge or stuff oneself
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Overeating with plenty of energy somehow builds muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Glute is informal shorthand for a gluteus, one of the large buttock muscles.

clue.text: Earth in wild tundra of specified disposition

indicators.note: wild suggests something unruly and out of order, so the letters are scrambled
one item placed in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: the letters of tundra rearranged
E is the standard abbreviation for earth

explanation.surface: A scene of soil out on the open, wild tundra.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside the rearranged NATURD, between R and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Natured is used in compounds such as good-natured, meaning having a temperament of the kind stated.

clue.text: Blame milkmaid that's pinched almost half the cream

indicators.note: a little less than half of the word is kept, so the rest is dropped
something pinched is taken and held, so the milkmaid word holds the other piece

parts.note: dey is an old word for a dairymaid
the first two of the five letters of cream, just under half

explanation.surface: A milkmaid is blamed for stealing a share of the cream.
explanation.walkthrough: Dey, an archaic word for a dairymaid, is found in Chambers. Cream has five letters, so two is just under half.
explanation.definitionFit: To decry is to condemn or censure publicly, close to blaming someone.

clue.text: Old pointer adopted subservient posture, we hear?

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken rather than written, so the sound matters

parts.note: to go down on one's knees is a subservient posture

explanation.surface: An old dog of the pointer breed lay down humbly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointer' suggests a dog; here it is a sharp pointed tool. Neeld is an obsolete spelling of needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Neeld is an archaic form of needle, a sharp-pointed sewing implement.

clue.text: Holding h-hand, played Acol, making contract?

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece encloses the other
the bidding system's name is played about with, so its letters are moved

parts.note: first part of the rearranged Acol, a British bridge bidding system
a mitt is a hand; the stammered h-hand doubles the first letter
the rest of the rearranged Acol

explanation.surface: A nervous bridge player, stammering over a hand, uses the Acol system to reach a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: Acol is a bidding system in bridge, where a contract is the bid you undertake. The stammer turns MITT into M-MITT, which goes inside COAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Committal means binding oneself to an undertaking, which is what making a contract involves.

clue.text: Fellow, in appearance elegant

indicators.note: one thing put in another sits inside it

parts.note: hue in the old sense of outward look or appearance
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A chap who looks stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elegant' is an old sense of the answer, as in the humane letters, meaning refined learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Humane once meant refined or polished, especially of learning, as in the humanities.

clue.text: The Magdalenian era, i.e. gender changing (11, two words)

indicators.note: changing means altering form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: the letters of these three words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A comment on how ideas of gender changed in some prehistoric period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Magdalenian' is the definition on its own, used as a noun for the period; 'era' belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Magdalenian culture of the late Old Stone Age is also called the reindeer age, after the animal its people hunted.

clue.text: Sang like Julie, famously, leaf fluttering in sward

indicators.note: a fluttering thing flaps about, so its letters move out of order
placed in the turf means sitting inside it

parts.note: sod is a piece of turf, part of a sward
the letters of leaf rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer on a lawn with a leaf blowing about, like Julie Andrews on an Alpine meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: Julie Andrews, as Maria in The Sound of Music, sang Do-Re-Mi on a hillside.
explanation.definitionFit: To sol-fa is to sing using do, re, mi syllables, as Julie Andrews famously did in Do-Re-Mi.

clue.text: Son, self-assertive, admitting bad wrong, getting punishment in camp?

indicators.note: wrong means not in proper order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one word takes the other inside

parts.note: a pushing person is forward and self-assertive
the letters of bad rearranged

explanation.surface: A pushy son who owns up to wrongdoing is punished at a summer camp.
explanation.walkthrough: The camp is a military one: peeling potatoes was a classic army fatigue given as a punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Spud-bashing is British forces slang for peeling potatoes, a chore given as a penalty in barracks or camp.

clue.text: Bird that's abandoned lake or …

definitions.note: the definition runs into the next clue: or … River

indicators.note: having abandoned something means leaving it behind, so a letter is removed

parts.note: ousel is a variant spelling of ouzel, the blackbird
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A bird has left the lake for the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on into the next clue, whose first word, River, completes this definition. OUSEL loses its L.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ouse is the name of several English rivers, including the Great Ouse and the Yorkshire Ouse.

clue.text: … River, with river craft around, something attached to schooner?

indicators.note: a thing placed around another encloses it

parts.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed river boat
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: a river scene with boats, and something tied to a sailing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside PUNT. A schooner is not the ship here but a large glass for sherry or beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A prunt is a blob of glass fused onto a drinking vessel as decoration, such as on a schooner glass.

clue.text: It's played in casinos, getting clubs on edge? Well!

parts.note: C is the card abbreviation for clubs
a hem is the edge of a cloth
both are exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A card player is on edge in a casino holding clubs, and exclaims.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemmy is a casual name for chemin de fer, a card game like baccarat played in casinos.

clue.text: Frame for drying cheese or fish

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dialect word for a rack or frame for drying cheeses
second meaning: a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A rack used to dry either cheese or fish, as on a farm or quay.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one rack for drying two foods, but the fish is a second sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hake is both a regional name for a drying rack, listed in Chambers, and a common food fish related to cod.

clue.text: Fool, headless chicken in court, in a stew

indicators.note: the pieces placed in the court sit inside it

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court

indicators.note: without a head means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: an ass is a fool
poule is French for hen

explanation.surface: A clown and a panicking chicken in a courtroom, everybody flustered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headless chicken' looks like the panicking idiom, but the chicken is French and simply loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassoulet is a slow-cooked French stew of beans with meats such as sausage, pork and duck.

clue.text: Old German dancer much employed

parts.note: an alma is an Egyptian dancing girl
in means in vogue, widely used

explanation.surface: A dancer from old Germany was in demand.
explanation.walkthrough: Alma (also almah) is a Chambers word for an Egyptian dancing girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Almain is an archaic word for a German, and also for the allemande dance.

clue.text: Like a pub with no beer that's captured attention?

definitions.text: Like a pub with no beer that's captured attention?

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor

parts.note: dry means without alcohol
to give ear is to give attention

explanation.surface: A beerless pub that has somehow got everyone listening.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'no beer' do double duty, inside the definition and in the wordplay. A Pub with No Beer is a famous Australian ballad about a gloomy pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub without beer is bleak and joyless, which is what dreary means.

clue.text: Part of garden I dug over and fed

indicators.note: turned over means the letters run the opposite way
part of a phrase means only some consecutive letters of it are used

parts.note: letters running across the end of garden, the I and the start of dug

explanation.surface: A gardener dug over a bed, then had a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug over' reads as digging the soil; 'over' is the signal to read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Dined and fed are both past forms of eating a meal.

clue.text: Body sees poorly — being so?

indicators.note: done poorly means done badly or out of order, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: the eight letters of these two words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A person whose eyesight is bad, and the question of why.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: someone who sees poorly may well be squint-eyed. Boss-eyed is British informal for having a squint.
explanation.definitionFit: Boss-eyed means having a squint or cross-eyes, a condition that gives poor or distorted vision.

clue.text: Bananas she iced burst open

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A baker iced bananas, which then split open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit being iced but is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To dehisce is the botanical term for a seed pod or fruit splitting open.

clue.text: Herd mostly restricts greeting for US gum

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one word encloses another
mostly means not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: beeves is an old plural of beef, meaning cattle
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A cattle herd hems in a greeting, all about American chewing gum.
explanation.walkthrough: BEEVES loses its S, then holds HI. In the American South, a gum or bee-gum is a hollowed gum-tree log used to house bees.
explanation.definitionFit: In US dialect a gum is a hive made from a hollow gum-tree log.

clue.text: Receivers of letters? From answers they can be found in

indicators.note: found in says the letters sit inside the words before

parts.note: letters spanning the end of From and the start of answers

explanation.surface: Mail recipients who appear among the answers.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are the epistles of St Paul, not post.
explanation.definitionFit: St Paul wrote an epistle to the Christians of Rome, so they were recipients of his letter.

clue.text: Bough twosome including linnet initially, then sandpiper

indicators.note: including means taking in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a duet is a pair of performers

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the bird's name

parts.note: first letter of linnet
a ree is a female ruff, a kind of sandpiper

explanation.surface: Two birds, a linnet and a sandpiper, perched on a branch.
explanation.walkthrough: Bough is an old word for the gallows; the ree is the female ruff.
explanation.definitionFit: A dule-tree is the Scots gallows tree, and bough was once used for the gallows too.

clue.text: Part of Bible oracle I mark beside patriarch's place

parts.note: Ur of the Chaldees was the home of Abraham
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A Bible prophecy is marked next to the place of a patriarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Urim and Thummim were objects worn by the Jewish high priest for consulting God, a kind of oracle.

clue.text: Cheese sample, e.g., wrapped by Tesco operative

indicators.note: something wrapped by other words is enclosed in them

parts.note: letters spanning the end of Tesco and the start of operative

explanation.surface: A supermarket worker hands out cheese tasters. Tesco is a large British supermarket chain.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'e.g.' marks the definition as an example: a cheese sample is one thing scooped.
explanation.definitionFit: A scoop is a portion taken out with a scoop, such as a cheese taster.

clue.text: Basin drying out regularly was situated in fort

indicators.note: something in a fort sits inside it

parts.note: a pa is a Maori fortified village
lay is the past tense of lie, to be situated

explanation.surface: A basin in an old fort dried up from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an every-other-letter signal but belongs to the definition. A pa is a Maori fortified village.
explanation.definitionFit: A playa is a desert basin that holds water after rain and then dries out to a flat bed.

clue.text: A sermon after church? One bracer after another!

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
taken as written
ser. is the abbreviation for sermon

explanation.surface: After a church sermon, the congregation heads for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come from 'A sermon after church', with CH first.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaser is a drink taken straight after another, such as a beer after a whisky, a bracer following a bracer.

clue.text: Catholic row over bishop, calling for one to succeed him

definitions.text: calling for one to succeed him

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Catholic
to row is to ply an oar
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A Catholic quarrel over a bishop leads to calls for his successor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'over' puts the oar on top of the bishop. Row as quarrel is the false path; here it is rowing a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarb was the successor of a saint as head of an early Irish monastery, so the role meant succeeding him.

clue.text: Spar? Broach boxing rule

indicators.note: boxing means putting in a box, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a broach is a roasting spit
R is the abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: A boxer asks about sparring and raises the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spar' and 'boxing' suggest a fight; a spar is a pole on a ship. R goes inside SPIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprit is a small spar running diagonally to extend a fore-and-aft sail.

clue.text: Millions in trawler's catch, one following little hooks

indicators.note: a thing put in another sits inside it

parts.note: a haul is a catch of fish
M is the abbreviation for millions
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Millions of small fish in a trawler's catch, one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: M goes inside HAUL, and I follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamuli is the plural of hamulus, an anatomical term for a small hook-shaped process.

clue.text: Webbing, soft, a priest put on behind

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft
taken as written
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist priest

explanation.surface: A priest dresses in soft woven fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A palama is the membrane between the toes of a water bird, its web.

clue.text: Special outfit for youngster

parts.note: SP is an abbreviation for special
a rig is an outfit of clothes

explanation.surface: A special set of clothes bought for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprig is an affectionate or dismissive term for a young person, an offshoot of the family.

clue.text: Curse of Scotland, partly seen in England?

indicators.note: partly says only some letters of the phrase are used

parts.note: letters spanning the end of seen, all of in and the start of England

explanation.surface: A Scottish curse that also turns up south of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: The curse of Scotland is a traditional name for the nine of diamonds playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: The nine of diamonds is nicknamed the curse of Scotland, for reasons historians still dispute.

clue.text: Old records from a Roman centre of industry

parts.note: taken as written
Roman Catholic, abbreviated RC
a hive is a busy centre, as in a hive of industry

explanation.surface: Historic documents from an ancient Roman industrial site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre of industry' looks like a middle-letter signal but is a whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An archive is a collection of historical documents and records.

clue.text: Migrant worker, a brilliant one, cutting big tree in pieces

indicators.note: broken in pieces means the letters are scattered
cutting into something means going inside it

parts.note: the letters of big tree rearranged
a brilliant performer is a star

explanation.surface: A star labourer from abroad chopping a large tree into bits.
explanation.walkthrough: A STAR goes inside the rearranged BIG TREE, after the G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastarbeiter is German for guest worker, a foreign labourer admitted to work in Germany.
